summary.text: Medieval Islamic astronomy covers the astronomical developments made in the Islamic world, especially during the Islamic Golden Age, and mostly written in Arabic.
It built on Greek, Sassanid, and Indian works that were translated and developed into a science with Islamic characteristics.
Latin translations of Arabic works in the 12th century helped revive ancient astronomy, and stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Deneb still carry Arabic names.

facts.value: The Islamic Golden Age, 9th to 13th centuries

facts.value: The first astronomical texts rendered into Arabic were Indian and Persian

source.title: Astronomy in the medieval Islamic world

paragraphs.heading: Astronomy in the Islamic world
paragraphs.text: Islamic astronomy means the study of the sky carried out in the Islamic world, mostly written in Arabic and above all during the 9th to 13th centuries. It happened mainly in the Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia and al-Andalus, and later in the Far East and India. Like other sciences of its time, it took in foreign material, especially Greek, Sassanid and Indian works. Those works were translated, built upon, and blended into a science with its own Islamic character.

paragraphs.heading: From star lore to mathematics
paragraphs.text: Before Islam, Arabs studied the sky by watching rather than calculating, unlike the Babylonians, Greeks and Indians, who had built detailed mathematical systems. They followed the rising and setting of certain stars, a local tradition known as Anwā’. After the coming of Islam, astronomers brought mathematics to this study of the night sky. The new faith also gave astronomy practical work: fixing the times of the five daily prayers and finding the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.

paragraphs.heading: Learning from India and Greece
paragraphs.text: The first astronomy books translated into Arabic came from India and Persia. The best known was the Zij al-Sindhind, made after 770 by al-Fazari and Ya'qub ibn Tariq from an Indian work, with help from Indian astronomers at the court of the caliph al-Mansur. Arab astronomers also adopted the Indian sine function, dropping the chords of arc that Greek trigonometry used. Ptolemy's Almagest, which placed a spherical Earth at the centre of the cosmos, was translated at least five times in the late 8th and 9th centuries and became the main authority.

paragraphs.heading: Baghdad's observatories
paragraphs.text: In early 9th-century Baghdad, the caliph al-Ma'mun gave strong backing to astronomy through the House of Wisdom, a public academy. He also built the first observatory in Baghdad, and more were later built in Iraq and Iran. In 830 the mathematician al-Khwarizmi produced the first major Muslim work of astronomy, with tables for the motions of the Sun, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. It brought Ptolemy's ideas into Islamic science and marked a turn from translating old books to developing new ideas.

paragraphs.heading: Checking Ptolemy's numbers
paragraphs.text: In 850 al-Farghani wrote a summary of Ptolemy's picture of the heavens, but he also corrected it using the findings of earlier Arab astronomers. He gave new values for the obliquity of the ecliptic, for the precession of the apogees of the Sun and Moon, and for the Earth's circumference. His book spread through the Muslim world and was translated into Latin. In the 10th century the Egyptian astronomer Ibn Yunus also found mistakes: where Ptolemy had the angle of the Earth's axial precession changing by one degree every 100 years, Ibn Yunus worked out one degree every 70¼ years.

paragraphs.heading: Doubts about Ptolemy
paragraphs.text: By the 10th century some texts doubted that Ptolemy was right, and scholars questioned whether the Earth really stood still at the centre of the universe. The polymath Ibn al-Haytham wrote Doubts on Ptolemy between 1025 and 1028; he kept the Earth-centred model but criticised parts of Ptolemy's theories. Other astronomers took up his challenge and built new models that solved the problems he had found. In 1070 al-Juzjani discussed the troubles with Ptolemy's theory of equants and offered a solution, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi also exposed problems in Ptolemy's work.

paragraphs.heading: A legacy in the night sky
paragraphs.text: About 10,000 manuscripts of Islamic astronomy survive, scattered around the world, and many have never been read or catalogued. Even so, a fairly accurate picture of the field can be pieced together. Its mark is still overhead today. Many stars, such as Aldebaran, Altair and Deneb, and terms such as azimuth and nadir, are still known by their Arabic names.
